title: Voting Rights Victory or Racial Gerrymandering? Louisiana's New Congressional Map
subtitle: Louisiana legislature passes new congressional map eliminating one of two majority-Black districts following Supreme Court ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act

conservative.headline: Louisiana GOP Passes Fair Congressional Map Following Supreme Court Ruling
conservative.byline: As seen on Washington Examiner, Daily Caller, PBS NewsHour
paragraphs: Louisiana has taken a bold step toward restoring constitutional principles in redistricting, passing a new congressional map that complies with the Supreme Court's landmark decision ending race-based gerrymandering.

The Louisiana legislature approved a 5-1 Republican map on May 29, following the Supreme Court's April 29 ruling in Louisiana v. Callais that struck down the state's previous configuration with two majority-Black districts. Writing for the 6-3 majority, Justice Samuel Alito made clear that allowing race to play any part in government decisionmaking represents a departure from the constitutional rule that applies in almost every other context.

The Washington Examiner editorial board celebrated the decision, noting that what has changed is that the Democratic Party can no longer use the Voting Rights Act as a reverse partisan gerrymander on purely racial grounds.

Republican State Senator Jay Morris, who sponsored the redistricting legislation, defended the new map as legally sound and constitutionally compliant. Morris emphasized that the state now has a map that meets all the traditional redistricting criteria and is not racially gerrymandered, expressing confidence it will be very defensible in court.

Morris was transparent about the partisan nature of the redistricting, acknowledging that he purposely put more Democrats into District 2 to make the remaining districts better performing for Republicans. This kind of partisan gerrymandering remains perfectly legal under Supreme Court precedent, unlike racial gerrymandering which the Court has now strictly limited.

Governor Jeff Landry echoed the colorblind constitutional framework embraced by the Court's conservative majority, declaring that the best way to end race-based discrimination is to stop making decisions based on race.

The Daily Caller characterized the new map as putting another remnant of institutionalized racism six feet under, framing the elimination of race-conscious districting as progress toward true equality.

The new map consolidates Democratic strength in New Orleans-based District 2, represented by Troy Carter, while creating five competitive Republican districts across the rest of the state. This configuration reflects Louisiana's genuine partisan makeup and ends the practice of using racial classifications to artificially engineer electoral outcomes.

Louisiana has shown the nation how to implement the Supreme Court's mandate: draw districts based on traditional redistricting criteria, respect communities of interest, and leave race out of the equation entirely.

liberal.headline: Louisiana Republicans Eliminate Majority-Black District to Grab House Seat
liberal.byline: As seen on PBS NewsHour, NPR, CNN
paragraphs: In a brazen act of voter suppression orchestrated by President Trump and enabled by the Supreme Court's conservative supermajority, Louisiana Republicans have eliminated a majority-Black congressional district and thrown away 40,000 already-cast ballots to secure partisan control.

Representative Troy Carter, whose New Orleans district survived the redistricting only after Republicans packed it with additional Democratic voters, condemned the cynical manipulation. Carter emphasized that no one's asking for extra rights, pointing out that discrimination remains very real in society and that suggesting otherwise is disingenuous at best.

The human cost of this political gamesmanship became clear when Carter spoke about the discarded ballots from the suspended May 16 primary. He noted that no one's vote should be thrown away, pointing out that 90-year-old voters who cast ballots may not be here for the rescheduled election, which represents the quintessential definition of irreparable harm.

Carter framed the stakes in constitutional terms, declaring that the question before us is whether we will honor the principle that every citizen deserves equal protection of the law, not merely about lines on a map.

Representative Cleo Fields, the Democrat losing his seat in the redistricting, traced the origins of the scheme directly to the White House. Fields revealed that when the president picked up the phone and called the governor of Texas and said I need five more Republican votes, he set in motion a coordinated assault on voting rights across the South.

Fields methodically dismantled the legal justifications for the rushed redistricting, noting that the Court's ruling didn't say you had to suspend the elections, didn't say Representative Carter's district had any problems, and didn't say Louisiana could not draw a second majority-Black district.

In a scathing dissent, Justice Elena Kagan warned of the consequences of the majority's decision, writing that states can now, without legal consequence, systematically dilute minority citizens' voting power.

Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene called the decision appalling and characterized it as the latest in a long line of attacks by President Donald Trump and the conservative court against the fundamental right of every American citizen to vote.

State Senator Royce Duplessis captured the moral dimension of Louisiana's actions, warning that the state is participating in a vicious race to the bottom that threatens to unravel decades of voting rights progress.

What Louisiana Republicans have done is not colorblind redistricting—it is a calculated erasure of Black political power dressed up in the language of constitutional principle, and it sets a dangerous precedent for voter suppression nationwide.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin
paragraphs: Both sides are presenting selective versions of the Louisiana redistricting story. Conservatives frame it as constitutional compliance while liberals see voter suppression. Here is what we actually know.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ Supreme Court Ruling: On April 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Louisiana v. Callais that the state's congressional map with two majority-Black districts was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, significantly limiting the scope of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.

✓ New Map Configuration: The legislature passed a new 5-1 Republican map on May 29-30, 2026, eliminating Representative Cleo Fields' majority-Black 6th district that stretched from Baton Rouge to Shreveport while preserving Representative Troy Carter's New Orleans-based 2nd district.
✓ Elections Suspended: Governor Jeff Landry suspended the May 16 congressional primaries after approximately 40,000 voters had already cast ballots. A new primary is scheduled for November 3, 2026.

✓ Demographics: Louisiana's population is approximately 33% Black. The old map had 4 Republicans and 2 Democrats (both from majority-Black districts). The new map creates 5 Republican-leaning districts and 1 Democratic district.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: This map is "colorblind" and doesn't consider race. Reality: State Senator Jay Morris openly admitted he consolidated Democrats (who are disproportionately Black in Louisiana) into District 2 to make other districts more Republican. The map's creators were acutely aware of racial demographics—they just used partisan justification rather than racial justification to achieve the desired outcome.

✓ Fair Point: The Supreme Court did rule that the previous two-district configuration violated the Constitution as the Court's majority now interprets it. Louisiana Republicans are implementing what the conservative Court majority mandated, and partisan gerrymandering remains legal under current precedent while racial gerrymandering does not.

⚠️ Claim: This ends "institutionalized racism" in redistricting. Reality: This is rhetorical reversal. The Voting Rights Act was passed specifically because Southern states used facially neutral rules to dilute Black voting power. Whether the current law goes too far in the other direction is debatable, but characterizing protections for minority voting strength as "institutionalized racism" inverts the historical context.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: Trump personally orchestrated this as part of a coordinated scheme. Reality: While Representative Fields alleges Trump called governors to demand more Republican seats, this remains unverified. What is documented is that multiple Southern states are redistricting following the Supreme Court decision, but attributing all of this to direct presidential coordination oversimplifies a complex legal and political process.

✓ Fair Point: The practical effect is undeniable—Black voting power in Louisiana is reduced. In a state that is 33% Black, having only one of six congressional districts where Black voters have meaningful influence does raise legitimate questions about proportional representation, regardless of the legal framework used to justify it.

⚠️ Claim: This is purely about voter suppression with no legitimate legal basis. Reality: The Supreme Court's conservative majority genuinely believes race-conscious redistricting violates equal protection principles. Whether you agree or not, this represents a coherent constitutional philosophy, not merely partisan hackery. The debate is about competing visions of equality: formal colorblindness versus substantive representation.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

This Louisiana redistricting fight exemplifies the fundamental tension in American voting rights law between two competing principles: the idea that government should never consider race in any form versus the reality that ignoring race can perpetuate the effects of historical discrimination. The Supreme Court's current majority has decisively chosen the former approach, reversing decades of precedent that prioritized the latter.

The discarded ballots represent a real cost of rushed redistricting—40,000 voters had their choices invalidated through no fault of their own. Both parties have used redistricting to gain advantage when in power, but the速度 and coordination of this Southern redistricting wave following the Court decision is unusual in scope.

What makes this story particularly contentious is that it perfectly illustrates how partisan gerrymandering and racial gerrymandering can produce identical results while falling on opposite sides of constitutional law. When Republican State Senator Morris says he packed Democrats into one district, and when critics say he diluted Black voting power, they're describing the same map—just using different legal frameworks.

The Bottom Line: Louisiana has redrawn its congressional map to eliminate a majority-Black district following a Supreme Court ruling that curtailed the Voting Rights Act. Whether you view this as constitutional compliance or voter suppression depends entirely on your philosophy about how government should address racial inequality—and that divide is precisely what makes this story so explosive.
